sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *hasta que* from A2 Unit 27, with the present subjunctive for a future limit (*Espero hasta que llegues*). The reason is the same as for *cuando*: the limit has not been reached yet, so it is only expected. When the limit was reached in the past, or it is a habit, the verb is a fact and takes the indicative.

sections.title: Future limit or fact?
rows: Me quedo aquí hasta que llegue el tren.
I'll stay here until the train arrives. (Future: subjunctive.)
Esperamos hasta que llegó el tren.
We waited until the train arrived. (A past fact: indicative.)
Todos los días trabaja hasta que cierran la oficina.
Every day he works until they close the office. (A habit: indicative.)

sections.title: New: the extra no
sections.content: In a negative sentence you will often hear a second *no* after *hasta que*: *No me voy hasta que no me paguen*. That *no* adds nothing, and the sentence means the same as *No me voy hasta que me paguen*: "I'm not leaving until they pay me". Do not translate it as "until they do not pay me". The mood does not change: it is still the subjunctive when you look ahead. You need to recognise this extra *no*; you do not have to use it.

items.spanish: Espero aquí hasta que me llamen.
items.english: I'll wait here until they call me.

items.spanish: No salgo de la oficina hasta que termine este informe.
items.english: I'm not leaving the office until I finish this report.

items.spanish: No te muevas hasta que yo te diga.
items.english: Don't move until I tell you.

items.spanish: No me voy hasta que no me paguen.
items.english: I'm not leaving until they pay me. (The second no adds nothing.)

sections.content: Always write *hasta que*, not *hasta* alone, before a verb with its own subject: *hasta que llegue*. *Hasta que* is not the same as *hasta* + a noun or a time, which you know from earlier units (*hasta las seis*, *hasta mañana*).
